title: When the Pour Stood Still — Cerebral Akinetopsia in Patient L.M., Random-Dot Signal-to-Noise Breakdown (Baker 1991), Post-Stroke Smooth-Pursuit Eye Tracking & Speed-Selective Reversal

teenKit.tldr: When a stroke damaged a specific region in Patient L.M.'s brain, she lost the ability to see motion, making pouring tea look like a solid glass glacier. This proves our brain processes movement completely separately from shapes and colors.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It shatters the illusion that our eyes are just video cameras, revealing that our perception of the world is actually a high-tech remix built by different neural departments working behind the scenes.
keyTakeaways: Cerebral akinetopsia, or motion blindness, completely strips the moving world of flow, turning continuous motion into a rapid series of frozen snapshots.
The brain handles movement in a specialized cinematic workshop called area V5/MT+, entirely separated from the circuits that recognize what an object actually is.
When visual motion processing fails, people have to hack their reality by using sound, weight shifts, and timing to guess what is happening right in front of them.

vocab.meaning: A rare neurological condition caused by brain damage that selectively deletes a person's ability to perceive physical motion.
A dangerous medical event where blood vessels rupture on both sides of the brain, flooding and damaging surrounding tissue.
The specific region in the visual cortex that acts as the brain's master hub for calculating speed and direction.
A visual test using swarms of moving dots used by scientists to measure how much visual noise a brain can handle before motion perception collapses.

quiz.question: If you had Patient L.M.'s condition (akinetopsia), what would happen if a car drove right past you?
options: The car would completely disappear from your sight until it stopped moving.
You would see the car instantly teleport to different positions without seeing it smoothly travel across the street.
You would see the car perfectly, but you wouldn't know it was a vehicle.
The car would look completely normal, but everything else in the background would be frozen.
quiz.explanation: Because motion processing is broken, the brain gets snapshots of the car's location rather than a smooth, continuous stream of movement.

quiz.question: How did Patient L.M. know when her teacup was full if she couldn't see the tea pouring?
options: She used infrared glasses that converted motion into heat maps.
She looked at the color changing inside the cup.
She relied on secondary clues like the changing sound of the liquid and the shifting weight in her hand.
She guessed purely by looking at the frozen glacier shape of the liquid.
quiz.explanation: Since visual motion feedback was totally gone, she had to crowdsource her survival clues from her ears and muscles.

quiz.question: What does the existence of motion blindness prove about how the human brain is organized?
options: Vision is processed as one single, unified stream where everything is recognized at the exact same time.
Motion and object recognition are processed by completely separate neural systems in the brain.
The brain cannot recover from any stroke that affects the visual cortex.
Hearing and touch are much more important for daily life than vision.
quiz.explanation: L.M. could still recognize objects and colors just fine, proving that movement perception has its own dedicated, independent neural real estate.
